landmarks.name: Kalandula Falls
landmarks.writeup: One of the largest waterfalls in Africa, located on the Lucala River, known for its impressive width and scenic beauty.

wiki.extract: Kalandula Falls or Calandula Falls are waterfalls in the municipality of Calandula, Malanje Province, Angola. On the Lucala River, the falls are 105 meters high and 400 meters wide. They are one of the largest waterfalls by volume in Africa. The distance from Luanda is 360 km (220 mi).

landmarks.name: Fortress of São Miguel
landmarks.writeup: A historic fort in Luanda built by the Portuguese in the 16th century, now housing the Museum of the Armed Forces.

wiki.extract: Fortaleza de São Miguel or Saint Michael Fortress was a Portuguese fortress built in 1576 in the Ingombota District of Luanda, Angola. During Dutch rule in Angola between 1641 and 1648, the fort was known as Fort Aardenburgh.

landmarks.name: Iona National Park
landmarks.writeup: Angola's largest national park, featuring diverse wildlife and unique desert landscapes.

wiki.extract: Iona National Park is the largest and oldest national park in Angola. It is situated in the Southwestern corner of the country, in Namibe Province. It is roughly bound by the Atlantic Ocean to the West, an escarpment to the East that marks the beginning of the interior plateau, the Curoca River to the North, and the Cunene River to the South. It is about 200 kilometres (120 mi) south of the city of Namibe and covers 5,850 square miles (15,200 km2) sq. miles.

landmarks.name: Mussulo Island
landmarks.writeup: A popular beach destination near Luanda, known for its sandy beaches and resorts.

wiki.extract: Mussulo is a peninsula located in south of Luanda Province, Angola. It was part of the municipality of Mussulo, province of Luanda, but was later made a municipality. It is actually a spit created by sediments from the Cuanza River, moved north by the Benguela Current. It is about 30 km long, at most 3 km wide, and at the narrowest parts in the south of the peninsula, less than 100 metres.

cultural_events.name: Carnaval de Luanda
cultural_events.writeup: An annual vibrant carnival featuring music, dance, and colorful parades reflecting Angolan culture.

wiki.extract: Ilha do Cabo typically known as Ilha de Luanda is a spit off the shore of Luanda, the capital of Angola, a country on the continents' southwestern coast. It consists of a low sandy strip formed by sedimentation. In administrative terms, the peninsula belongs to the municipality of Ingombota in the Luanda Province.

cultural_events.name: Festa da Independência
cultural_events.writeup: Celebrated on November 11th, marking Angola's independence from Portugal in 1975 with various cultural activities.

wiki.extract: The Independence Day of Brazil, commonly called Sete de Setembro, is a national holiday observed in Brazil on 7 September of every year. The date celebrates Brazil's Declaration of Independence from the United Kingdom of Portugal, Brazil and the Algarves on 7 September 1822.

food_writeup: Angolan cuisine blends African, Portuguese, and Brazilian influences, featuring dishes like funge (a cassava or cornmeal porridge), moamba de galinha (chicken stew with palm oil), and fresh seafood.
brief_history: Angola was a Portuguese colony from the late 16th century until 1975. After independence, it experienced a prolonged civil war until 2002. Since then, Angola has been rebuilding its economy, largely driven by oil and diamond resources.
current_conflicts: Angola is currently stable with no major internal conflicts, focusing on post-war reconstruction and economic development.

commentary.inflation_management: Angola's inflation is a mirror of the oil price and the kwanza. It ran in double digits through the boom (12-14% in 2006-2011), then fell to a series low of 7.3% in 2014 as oil peaked. The 2014 oil crash forced repeated kwanza devaluations and, in 2018, a shift toward a more flexible exchange rate under the IMF program; inflation exploded to 30.7% in 2016 and 29.8% in 2017. Tighter policy under the 2018 IMF arrangement brought it down to 17.1% by 2019, but shocks kept coming: 22.3% in 2020, 25.8% in 2021, and after another kwanza slide in 2023, inflation surged again to 28.2% in 2024, easing to a projected 20.2% in 2025. The central bank has hiked rates aggressively at each turn, but pass-through from the exchange rate dominates outcomes.
commentary.debt_management: Angola's debt trajectory tracks the oil cycle with a lag. From 16.7% of GDP in 2006 it was contained through the boom, but the 2014 crash and kwanza depreciation drove it from 35.4% (2014) to a crushing 119.8% of GDP in 2020, the series high, with much of it dollar-linked Chinese and Eurobond debt. The December 2018 IMF Extended Fund Facility (about $3.7 billion) anchored fiscal consolidation, debt reprofiling, and exchange-rate flexibility; combined with the 2021-22 oil rebound, debt fell sharply to 57.3% in 2022. Another oil-price and currency wobble pushed it back to 75.6% in 2023 before easing to a projected 50.9% in 2025. Sustainability has improved but remains hostage to oil and the kwanza.

key_events.event: Oil price crash: GDP in USD terms peaked at $164.4bn (2014) then collapsed; debt and inflation surged.
Joao Lourenco succeeded Jose Eduardo dos Santos after 38 years, launching an anti-corruption drive (Isabel dos Santos assets frozen in the 2020 'Luanda Leaks' fallout).
IMF approved a three-year Extended Fund Facility of about $3.7 billion (December 7, 2018); kwanza moved to a more flexible regime.
COVID-19 and an oil price collapse pushed debt to 119.8% of GDP, the series peak; IMF augmented the program.
Lourenco narrowly won re-election; oil rebound cut debt to 57.3% of GDP.
Kwanza slide and OPEC production cuts re-accelerated debt and inflation (28.2% in 2024).

commentary.outlook_next_decade: The base case is oil-dependent stabilization: with the IMF program completed and debt back near 50% of GDP, Angola has breathing room, but another oil downturn would quickly reverse it. Upside depends on diversification and the long-promised new oil licensing rounds offsetting declining mature fields; downside is kwanza volatility reigniting the inflation-debt spiral. Uncertainty is moderate-to-high given oil concentration and the opacity of Chinese bilateral debt.
commentary.caveat: Outlook is an analytical assessment as of October 2026, not a forecast. 2025 figures are IMF estimates/projections.
